Seif katan 2, "they bow," etc. Rama writes that one should pause between "He will not save" and the word "but we," so that "but we" should not appear to refer back to the preceding statement, as though, God forbid, we too were joining ourselves with the nations of the lands.

"All the Kaddishes." Meaning those that we call the prayer Kaddishes, such as the Kaddish after Aleinu. "To cast lots" means between one observing a yahrzeit and the mourners.

"It belongs to the mourners unless there is a yahrzeit," etc. Meaning a person whose yahrzeit falls on Shabbos has a claim to the Kaddish of Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbos. If his yahrzeit was on Friday, however, he has no claim to that Kaddish, because Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbos belongs specifically to Shabbos. Even according to our practice, under which reciting the psalm itself does not yet constitute acceptance of Shabbos until Barechu is recited, the psalm nevertheless belongs specifically to Shabbos. I later saw that Baer Heitev writes the same in the name of a manuscript responsum.

There is a proof from the beginning of the second chapter of Yoma. Although the kohanim cast lots for all the services in the Beit HaMikdash to determine who would merit each service, the Sages initially did not institute a lottery for terumat hadeshen in the morning. Only after they saw that the matter had led to danger did they institute a lottery. The Gemara explains that because terumat hadeshen was performed before dawn, while it was still night, it was initially thought that the kohanim would not regard it as sufficiently important to quarrel over, since the other services are performed by day. They therefore assumed that no lottery was needed and whoever wished could perform it. Another reason was that because it was done before dawn, sleep would deter many kohanim from coming, and there would be no reason to expect a quarrel. If many nevertheless came, they would race up the 32-amah ramp, and whoever first entered the 4 amot nearest the altar would merit the service. If 2 arrived equally within those 4 amot, the official told them, "Extend a finger." Rashi and R' Ovadiah of Bartenura explain that all the kohanim would extend a finger. The official would choose a number, and the kohen upon whom the count ended would merit the service. The count cycled around their fingers, because it is forbidden to count Jews directly.

Thus, the 2 who had reached the final 4 amot equally were the actual contenders for the service, and nevertheless the lottery was conducted with all the kohanim. Eliyah Rabbah rejects this proof, arguing that the case is different because a lottery cannot properly be conducted between only 2 people. He cites Tosafot Yom Tov, who explains that if there were only 2 fingers, once the official chose whether the number was even or odd and one knew where the count began, the result would effectively be predetermined, so it would not be a genuine lottery.

This rejection, however, is not conclusive. Tosafot Yom Tov wrote this only to explain why Rashi and R' Ovadiah of Bartenura understood "extend a finger" as directed to all the kohanim rather than only to the 2 who arrived together. If the official who selected the number also began the counting, then with only 2 contenders he could choose in advance who would win by choosing an even or odd number. Even according to Rambam and Ritva, who hold that the person who selected the number did not himself begin the count, so that even among 2 there could theoretically have been uncertainty, the language "extend a finger" implies a true lottery of the ordinary kind, and the normal lottery included the larger group. The comparison therefore remains relevant to our case: even when only certain individuals have the primary claim, the lottery can include all those whose rights are implicated by the distribution.

The purpose of casting lots among those entitled to Kaddish is to preserve peace and establish an orderly division where several mourners or a yahrzeit claimant have competing rights. One must therefore distinguish among the Kaddishes themselves, because not every yahrzeit has a claim to every Kaddish. A yahrzeit on Shabbos has a claim to Kaddish associated with a Shabbos passage, whereas a yahrzeit from Friday does not acquire a claim merely because the Kaddish is recited after Shabbos has begun. Likewise, the ordinary mourners retain their established rights to the mourner's Kaddishes except where the yahrzeit has precedence according to the accepted order.

Where a lottery is required, it should be a genuine lottery rather than an arrangement whose result can be manipulated. This follows from the discussion in Yoma. The fact that the 2 equal contenders were the ones entitled to the service did not prevent all the kohanim from participating in the counting mechanism. Thus, there is no objection to including the relevant group in the procedure used to determine which claimant receives the Kaddish.

The distinctions concerning mourners are also governed by the mourner's stage of mourning and by the nature of the Kaddish. A mourner during shivah has a stronger claim than one who is later in the mourning period, and a mourner during sheloshim has a stronger claim than one who is beyond sheloshim, subject to the customary rules regarding a mourner for a father or mother. A yahrzeit has its particular precedence on the day of the anniversary, but this does not erase all rights of the mourners. Where several people have equal standing, they cast lots or divide the Kaddishes in accordance with the established communal custom.

The same general principle applies to a resident and a guest. The regular rights attached to the congregation belong first to those who are part of that congregation, while a guest's claim is evaluated according to the accepted customs of precedence. Yet the purpose of the rules is not to deprive a mourner of Kaddish, but to distribute the available Kaddishes fairly and without quarrel. Where the community has a fixed custom, that custom determines the allocation unless it contradicts an explicit rule.

All of these details concern the Kaddishes that are distributed among mourners and yahrzeit observers. They are not a license to multiply Kaddishes without need. The established prayers and Kaddishes are to be recited in their proper places, with the rights of the mourners arranged by the rules of precedence, equality, and lottery explained above. The central concern is that the merit intended for the deceased be obtained without creating dispute among the living, and that each person receive the Kaddish to which he is entitled under the accepted order.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; long Kaddish-priority discussion translated and normalized.
